meta.title: Who really said "Imperfect action is better than perfect inaction"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No evidence Harry Truman ever said it. Etymologist Barry Popik dates the exact wording to 2005; the nearest ancestor is a 1947 line by John Collier.

meta.ogDescription: Truman gets the credit, but no source exists. Popik found the exact phrase in print only from 2005, and a longer ancestor in John Collier's 1947 book.

answer.label: Not Harry S. Truman — an unsourced modern maxim
answer.authorDates: Earliest documented wording 1947 · exact phrase in print by 2005 · credited to Truman online from 2009
answer.sourceLine: No Truman speech, letter, diary or book has ever been produced for this line. Etymologist Barry Popik ↗, who traced the phrase, states flatly that it is “frequently credited to Harry S. Truman (1884-1972), but there is no evidence that he ever said it.” The nearest documented ancestor is a longer, differently worded sentence in John Collier’s The Indians of the Americas (1947); the exact modern wording only reaches print in 2005, in two business and publishing self-help books.

source.excerpt: No matter what you do, don’t idle too long wondering about what to do—just do something! Imperfect action is better than perfect inaction.
trail: The finding. Etymologist Barry Popik ↗ investigated the phrase and concluded it is “frequently credited to Harry S. Truman (1884-1972), but there is no evidence that he ever said it.” Popik is a contributor-consultant to the OED, the Dictionary of American Regional English and The Yale Book of Quotations ↗.

1947 — the nearest ancestor. Popik’s earliest citation is John Collier’s The Indians of the Americas (W. W. Norton, 1947) ↗, page 281: “Imperfect action is better for men and societies than perfection in waiting, for the errors wrought by action are cured by new action.” It shares the opening words and the argument, but not the epigram — and Popik draws no causal line between the two.

1985 to 2005 — the wording tightens. Popik records “IMPERFECT action is far better than perfect inaction” in The Daily Herald (Chicago) on 12 September 1985, and the exact modern sentence in two 2005 books. None of these attaches a name to it at all, let alone Truman’s.

The sourced record stays empty. The line is absent from Wikiquote’s Truman entry ↗ in every section, and the talk-page question raised on 13 October 2013 ↗ has drawn no reply. Popik’s earliest Truman-credited example is a tweet of 2 November 2009.
source.excerptNote: This is one of the two 2005 books in which Popik documents the exact modern wording — Build It Big: 101 Insider Secrets from Top Direct Selling Experts (Chicago: Dearborn Trade Pub.), p. 106. The other is Pat Walsh’s 78 Reasons Why Your Book May Never Be Published (Penguin, 2005): “In other words, imperfect action is better than perfect inaction.” Neither book credits Truman. Popik’s intermediate citation, from The Daily Herald (Chicago) of 12 September 1985, reads “IMPERFECT action is far better than perfect inaction.”

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for this sentence, because no one has identified who wrote it or where it first appeared — and a quotation with no located source cannot be shown to be public domain. Separately, the nearest documented ancestor, John Collier’s The Indians of the Americas, was first published in 1947 by W. W. Norton, so even that earlier wording falls well after the pre-1931 line for U.S. public domain and should be treated as in copyright.

author.name: John Collier
author.kicker: Nearest documented ancestor — not the author of the maxim
author.heading: The 1947 sentence that came first
author.bio: John Collier ran the Bureau of Indian Affairs under Franklin Roosevelt and was the architect of the 1934 Indian Reorganization Act. In The Indians of the Americas (New York: W. W. Norton, 1947), page 281, he wrote the earliest wording Popik documents in this family: “Imperfect action is better for men and societies than perfection in waiting, for the errors wrought by action are cured by new action.” That is a philosophy of governing, not a motivational slogan — and no researcher has shown a chain connecting it to the short epigram now pinned on Truman, so Collier should be read as the closest known ancestor rather than the author.

misattribution.heading: How Truman got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a clean case of a modern motivational maxim reverse-engineered onto a famously decisive president. There is no disputed manuscript, no contested transcript, no rival claimant — just an unsourced line and a name that makes it sound authoritative.

items.why: Barry Popik ↗ — a freelance contributor-consultant to the Oxford English Dictionary, the Dictionary of American Regional English and The Yale Book of Quotations — states the phrase is “frequently credited to Harry S. Truman (1884-1972), but there is no evidence that he ever said it.” The earliest crediting to Truman he records is a tweet dated 2 November 2009. Truman died in 1972.

The line does not appear anywhere on Wikiquote’s Truman page ↗ — not in the sourced quotes, not in Disputed, not in Misattributed. On the talk page ↗, editor Chad Schultz asked on 13 October 2013 whether Truman originated it, saying he had found “nothing reliable indicating he actually said it.” The question sits there unanswered.

items.who: “Imperfect action beats perfect inaction every time”
items.why: A second, punchier phrasing circulates under the same name — AZQuotes credits it to Harry S. Truman ↗ as well, with no source. Free-floating wording is a hallmark of a quote with no original text to anchor it.

Wikiquote’s Misattributed section ↗ records that the desk sign “The buck stops here!” did not originate with Truman, that he popularised rather than coined “If you can’t stand the heat, get out of the kitchen,” and that “If you want a friend in Washington, get a dog” apparently comes from Samuel Gallu’s 1975 play Give ’Em Hell, Harry. Truman attracts aphorisms he never produced.

Goodreads ↗ serves the line under Truman’s name while carrying its own disclaimer that “Quotes are added by the Goodreads community and are not verified by Goodreads.” That is the whole citation chain most repostings rest on.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody knows who wrote it. Per Popik’s chronology ↗, the exact sentence is not documented in print until 2005 — in Pat Walsh’s 78 Reasons Why Your Book May Never Be Published and in Build It Big: 101 Insider Secrets from Top Direct Selling Experts. It is a piece of late-20th-century business-motivational language, not a presidential utterance.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Truman
lead: Truman is a magnet for decisiveness quotes because his actual reputation fits them. He kept a sign reading The buck stops here on his Oval Office desk, and his public image — the plain-spoken Missourian who made enormous decisions quickly — is exactly the personality a slogan about acting before you are ready wants to borrow. A maxim credited to Truman arrives pre-loaded with authority.

But that same magnetism is why Wikiquote’s Truman entry needs a whole Misattributed section ↗. The desk sign was mailed to him, not coined by him; “If you can’t stand the heat, get out of the kitchen” he popularised rather than originated; and “If you want a friend in Washington, get a dog” appears to come from a 1975 stage play about him. “Imperfect action is better than perfect inaction” is the same phenomenon, one step further along: it never touched Truman at all.
detailsBody: The thought itself is genuinely old, which is part of why the modern phrasing feels like a rediscovered classic rather than a workshop slogan. Wikipedia’s article on “Perfect is the enemy of good” ↗ traces the family back through Voltaire, who quoted the Italian proverb Il meglio è l’inimico del bene in his Questions sur l’Encyclopédie in 1770, to Montesquieu around 1726, and to the Duke of Albany in King Lear (1606): “striving to better, oft we mar what’s well.” That article does not mention Truman or this quote.

Popik also flags a modern sibling: “Done is better than perfect,” often credited to Sheryl Sandberg. The idea is common property. Only the specific 14-syllable packaging is recent — and it is that packaging, not the idea, that has been hung on a president who died in 1972.
context.pull: The line sounds like Truman because we already believe Truman would have said it. That is what a quote magnet is.

sourcesVerified.claim: Popik states the quote is frequently credited to Harry S. Truman (1884-1972) but there is no evidence he ever said it; his citations are John Collier's The Indians of the Americas (1947) p. 281, The Daily Herald (Chicago) 12 September 1985, and two 2005 books (Pat Walsh's 78 Reasons... and Build It Big p. 106); earliest Truman-credited example is a tweet of 2 November 2009; page dated March 28, 2014.

Wikiquote's Harry S. Truman page contains no instance of 'imperfect' or 'inaction' in any section; its Misattributed section does document 'The buck stops here!', 'If you can't stand the heat, get out of the kitchen' and 'If you want a friend in Washington, get a dog' (traced to Samuel Gallu's 1975 play Give 'Em Hell, Harry).

A talk-page section titled with this quote, posted by Chad Schultz at 18:45, 13 October 2013 (UTC), says he found 'nothing reliable indicating he actually said it' and asks who originated it; no reply follows before the next section.
John Collier lived May 4, 1884 – May 8, 1968, was 33rd Commissioner of Indian Affairs from 1933 to 1945, and wrote The Indians of the Americas (New York: W. W. Norton, 1947).

The Internet Archive holds a scan of John Collier's The Indians of the Americas dated 1947 (identifier indiansofamerica0000john_v6w8); full-text search inside it is restricted, so the page-281 wording is cited on Popik's authority rather than read directly.

Goodreads presents 'Imperfect action is better than perfect inaction.' as a quote by Harry S. Truman, alongside its own notice that 'Quotes are added by the Goodreads community and are not verified by Goodreads.'
AZQuotes credits the variant wording 'Imperfect action beats perfect inaction every time.' to Harry S. Truman.

The article documents Voltaire quoting the Italian proverb 'Il meglio è l'inimico del bene' in Questions sur l'Encyclopédie (1770), Montesquieu around 1726, and King Lear (1606) 'striving to better, oft we mar what's well'; it does not mention Truman or 'imperfect action is better than perfect inaction'.
Barry Popik is 'a freelance contributor-consultant to the Oxford English Dictionary, Dictionary of American Regional English, Historical Dictionary of American Slang and The Yale Book of Quotations.'
